routeName: Fingle Bridge River Walk (5 Mile Loop)
routeDescription: Fingle Bridge is a brilliant river-and-woods walk if you want children to feel like they're properly out in the wild, without losing the reassurance of a pub, parking and toilets near the bridge. The riverside paths, packhorse bridge, woodland, meadows and weir give children plenty to notice, and wildlife spotters should look out for kingfishers, otters, salmon and brown trout in the clear water below. The full Teign Gorge loop has steep sections, steps and muddy ground, so it's better for walkers (or backcarriers) than buggies. For an easier family version, stay lower along the river and use Fingle Bridge as the anchor point for snacks, paddling pauses and a shorter out-and-back.

Stepping stones, clear water and the chance to spot salmon and kingfishers keep children entertained at their own pace. Pack layers and decent shoes, and keep younger children close near the river and road crossing by the bridge.

routeName: River Otter Walk - Tipton St John
routeDescription: This is a proper half-day family walk in its entirety rather than a quick wander, running about five miles from Tipton St John towards Ottery St Mary and back along public footpaths on both sides of the river. It's mostly fairly flat with small climbs over bridges and stiles, so older children who can manage the distance should get a good mix of river, countryside, bridges and village interest. The River Otter is home to England's first legally reintroduced wild beavers — keep an eye out for gnawed trees and dams as evidence of their activity, and at dusk there's a real chance of spotting them feeding. Build in snacks, mud-ready shoes and a play at the playpark in Tipton as an incentive; for younger children, it may work better as a shorter out-and-back from one end.

routeDescription: Aylesbeare Common is a quieter, wilder walk for children who enjoy nature spotting more than play equipment. There are two signed trails — a short 0.75-mile route and a longer 3-mile route — with heathland, birds, butterflies, dragonflies and seasonal colour. Heath spotted orchids and bog plants like sundew add to the nature interest, and the hilltop position gives lovely views from either side of the reserve. The longer trail can be uneven, with gradients, steps and gates, so choose the shorter or tarmac farm-track option across the road from the main car park if legs are small and tire quickly. There are no toilets here, so plan it as a fresh-air-and-wildlife stop rather than a facilities-based outing.

routeDescription: The Goat Walk is an easy win when you want estuary views, boats, birdlife and a quaint Topsham feel without committing to a long walk. The circular route is around 2–2.5 miles, mostly flat and well-surfaced, making it ideal for scooters, balance bikes and early cyclists as well as buggies. The narrow waterside section is beautiful but needs care with scooters, buggies and small children because parts sit right beside the estuary with no railing. The RSPB bird hide along the route is a great spot for avocet and wading bird watching, and the quayside at the end offers cafés, pubs, toilets and independent shops. Works well as a loop or a relaxed out-and-back with a stop for snacks at the quay.

routeName: Exe Estuary Trail - Exmouth to Lower Halsdon Farm
routeDescription: This is a useful short stretch of the Exe Estuary Trail when you want the views and fresh air without committing to a long ride or walk. From Exmouth, the route quickly picks up the shared tarmac path towards Lower Halsdon Farm, with the estuary opening out beside you and Avocet Line trains running along the waterline — a bonus for train-loving children. It's good for buggies, scooters, balance bikes and early cyclists because the path is flat and well-surfaced, though it is shared with faster cyclists and walkers, so younger children may need reminding to keep left and watch for passing riders. Lower Halsdon Farm's National Trust tea garden makes a lovely turnaround point, open weekends from May to September.

Carter Avenue play park in Exmouth sits just before the main road near the end and makes a useful incentive or a natural turning point if you're doing an out-and-back.

routeDescription: A lovely Exmouth seafront stretch when you want a walk that feels coastal without being complicated. routeDescription: The Byes is one of the easiest riverside routes to use with children because it feels peaceful and tucked away, but still connects back into Sidmouth and the high street. The path follows the River Sid — Devon's shortest river — for about 1.5 miles through meadows and parkland towards Sidford, and is tarmacked throughout, making it good for scooters, bikes and buggies. Multiple small bridges cross the river along the route, which children tend to make the most of. Keep an eye out for kingfishers, dippers and grey wagtails, and otters are present in the river too. Build it around a town café, play stop or beach visit at the end — continuing into Sidmouth brings you out at Ham Play Park and the far end of the town beach, with cafés and ice cream a short walk away.

routeDescription: Bellever gives families a proper Dartmoor woodland outing without having to head straight onto open moor. The East Dart River runs along the edge of the forest and fills up in summer with families picnicking and paddling on its banks — get there early on warm days as the best spots go quickly. There are several waymarked trails to choose from: a short easy-access path from the car park straight to the river, a history trail past Bronze Age hut circles, and a longer route up to Bellever Tor with wide views across the moor. Heritage Dartmoor Ponies graze the forest throughout the year — children love seeing them, but keep your distance and don't feed them. Toilets at the car park, open 9:30am–5pm. Parking is paid but cheap.

routeDescription: Parke is a lovely National Trust estate when you want a proper walk without paying for a big house-and-garden day. The riverside paths, woodland, pasture, orchard and old railway line give you lots of ways to shape the visit: a short loop, a muddier stomp, a bike-friendly stretch on the Wray Valley Trail, or a slower wander to spot wildlife by the River Bovey. It's best in boots after wet weather. The paths from the main car park aren't smooth, so off-road buggies and backcarriers work better than standard pushchairs. There's a small café near the car park with toilets, the river route has good shade and picnic spots — bring a blanket — and there are plenty of places to paddle if children find the water.

routeDescription: Bystock Pools is a peaceful nature reserve with ponds, heathland, meadows and woodland, managed by Devon Wildlife Trust. In spring and summer the dragonflies and damselflies around the water are the big draw — there are rare species here including the southern damselfly. The reserve also has ducks on the upper ponds, grazing ponies further in, and butterflies in the heathland margins. It has that quiet, hidden-away feel in all seasons, but it's not suited to buggies — the paths are narrow and uneven in places, so it's one for determined legs or a good backcarrier. No facilities on site at all, so bring snacks and make sure younger children are comfortable before you set off.

routeDescription: Blackbury Camp is at its best in bluebell season — usually late April to mid-May — when the woodland inside and around the Iron Age hillfort fills with bluebells in a way that genuinely stops you in your tracks. The hillfort itself is small, compact and free to enter: children can run the ramparts, explore the earthworks and find the southern barbican entrance, which is unusually well preserved. The flat interior is good for picnics and ball games. Paths can be uneven and muddy, so it's boots and slow exploring rather than scooters or polished facilities. No café or toilets at the site — Blackbury Honey Farm is a short drive away if you want a stop on the way out. The narrow lanes to get there need careful driving.

routeDescription: A free self-guided walking trail around Exmouth town, spotting life-sized dinosaur models, murals and etchings scattered across the streets and seafront. There are two versions — a shorter Town Trail and a longer Explorer Trail — both starting from the Tourist Information Centre on The Strand, where you can pick up a free trail map. Brass rubbing plaques sit alongside each dinosaur, and children who complete all the rubbings can collect a souvenir badge from the TIC for £1. Species include velociraptors, a brachiosaurus, iguanodon, ichthyosaur and a T-Rex hatching from an egg. The trail also links to the Ordnance Survey Secret Stories app if you want to go digital, which adds clues, Horrible Histories-style stories and puzzles along the route.

routeDescription: Haldon's easiest family trail: a 1.5-mile loop on a wide, fully surfaced path through conifers, with open viewpoints, shelters, benches and picnic spots along the way. It's the most manageable choice for pushchairs, manual wheelchairs, beginner cyclists and young children who want forest time without a long walk. The current activity trail running along this route is Room on the Broom — interactive panels help children find Witch's lost hat, bow and wand and collect spell ingredients, with a trail pack available from the info pod for £4. The Gruffalo orienteering challenge also runs alongside it: pick up the separate £1.50 map from the info pod to find 12 hidden markers around the route. Both are worth knowing about before you visit so children can choose, or do both. Note there are two road crossings along the route, and paths can get muddy after rain, so wellies are a good idea in wetter months.

routeDescription: The gentlest cycling option at Haldon: a fully surfaced, mostly level shared trail that works well for newer riders, balance-bike graduates and families cycling together. It follows the same wide path as the walking Discovery Trail, passing viewpoints, shelters and picnic areas through the conifers. It's shared with walkers and other cyclists, so it suits riders who can slow down and pass carefully, and there are two road crossings to manage. A good first forest ride for children still building confidence before moving to singletrack. Helmets required.

routeDescription: Danes Wood is the quieter, wilder side of Killerton for families who want woodland rather than gardens. Ancient oaks and sweet chestnuts make it proper climbing-tree territory, and the exposed sandstone quarry banks around the edges give children something interesting to scramble on and explore. The interior of the wood is open access land so there's no set route to follow, which suits children who want to poke around at their own pace. In spring it earns its local reputation as a bluebell walk, and the wildlife is good year-round — songbirds in the canopy, butterflies in the clearings, and fungi worth looking for in autumn. After rain the paths get properly muddy, so it's better suited to wellies rather than trainers. There are no facilities beyond the small free car park, which actually makes it feel like more of a proper woodland adventure, but worth keeping in mind.

routeDescription: Killerton works well for families because you can scale the visit to the day you're having. A short wander near the house and café is a workable simple option, but there are also parkland paths, the Iron Age hill fort on Dolbury Hill, woodland routes out to Danes Wood and longer loops through the estate that keep older children properly occupied. Children who like the idea of climbing an extinct volcano will enjoy heading up to The Clump, where the legend of a friendly dragon living inside the hill is worth telling on the way up. The estate also has orienteering courses, including the Volcano Challenge for children aged eight and over, available for 50p from visitor reception. With the café, toilets, second-hand bookshop and shop all at the main visitor hub, it's one of the easier full-day outdoor options in East Devon, particularly if you're already a National Trust member.

routeDescription: Columbjohn is one of the more satisfying Killerton routes for older children who can manage a proper walk. It takes you beyond the obvious visitor areas into parkland, woodland and quieter estate paths, with the River Culm, old trees and the tiny private chapel at Columbjohn giving the route a sense of history and discovery. routeDescription: This route gives children the satisfaction of actually travelling somewhere rather than completing a loop. The flat, well-surfaced path runs from Killerton through farmland and quiet lanes to Clyston Mill in Broadclyst, one of the South West's last remaining watermills, and then on into the village itself if you want a further destination. The route crosses the M5 on a bridge, which children tend to find particularly exciting, and Broadclyst village has a play park, pub and village shop at the far end. Clyston Mill is free for NT members and worth building in if it's open. The path is flat and surfaced enough for bikes and scooters, and the six-mile return trip is manageable for most families with a reasonable pace and a snack stop.

routeDescription: The Beer to Branscombe route follows the South West Coast Path across cliff tops and through woodland, with wide sea views and Branscombe giving the walk a clear destination. The outward section from Beer climbs to Beer Head before dropping via 83 steps down to Branscombe Mouth, so legs need to be willing as this is not a flat or gentle walk. The return via the Hooken Undercliff is one of the more dramatic stretches of the Jurassic Coast: a ten-acre landslip that broke away from the cliff in 1790, leaving chalk pinnacles and a mysterious tangled wilderness that children tend to find properly interesting. Branscombe has pubs, a National Trust tea room and a working forge to pause at, and the 899 bus runs back to Beer if legs give out at the end. Note that as of early 2026, one section of the coast path near the Hooken was subject to a closure due to subsidence, so it's worth check the South West Coast Path website before visiting.

routeDescription: A flat, open estuary route with wide skies, water on both sides in places, and the Turf pub sitting at the end as a genuine destination rather than just a turning point. The Turf is one of the few pubs in the country you genuinely cannot reach by car only on foot, by bike or by boat, which gives the journey a sense of purpose that children respond to well. The route follows the Exe Estuary Trail along the canal towpath, with boats, lock gates, birdlife and estuary views keeping things interesting along the way. It feels more exposed than a woodland walk, so wind and weather make a difference to how enjoyable it is. The Topsham Ferry runs from late April to September, which gives you the option of a one-way trip with a ferry return if the distance feels like too much on the way back.

routeDescription: The Turf Locks sit where the Exeter Ship Canal meets the Exe Estuary, and the appeal for families is straightforward: lock gates to peer into, boats coming through, wide estuary views, good birdwatching and a proper pub garden at the end that welcomes children and dogs without fuss. routeDescription: A calm, flat riverside walk from Budleigh Salterton along the River Otter to Otterton Mill, with birdwatching, beaver evidence and the mill as a natural destination at the far end. The path is mostly level and well-surfaced near Budleigh, with bird hides and viewing points early on — children enjoy the peek holes in the hides for scanning the reedbeds. You are unlikely to spot a beaver on the water, but the gnawed trees and felled trunks along the riverbank are unmissable evidence of their presence, which children may find exciting. The full route to Otterton Mill and back is about six miles, so it suits families with older children or confident walkers; a shorter out-and-back to the first bridge makes a more manageable version for younger legs, and the path can get boggy after rain so wellies are worth considering. Otterton Mill has a café and cream teas at the end if you make the full distance.

routeDescription: Woodbury Castle gives families an easy way into Woodbury Common without needing to commit to a long walk. routeDescription: Woodbury Common is a wide open landscape of heathland, pine edges, rough tracks and long views, and its appeal for families is mainly in the freedom rather than any specific feature. The stony paths further from the car parks don't suit bikes unless they're proper off-road, but the tracks closer in work for a determined balance biker or remote-controlled monster truck. routeDescription: A short, unhurried walk around Lympstone village that takes in the harbour, historic buildings, Peter's Tower and the estuary foreshore. The harbour is the main draw for children — the passages between the cottages lead down to the beach, where the houses back right onto the shore and the residents close metal flood gates at high tide, and the harbour where (timed right) children can go crabbing. The tall poles on the beach traditionally used for drying washing and still stand today, and Peter's Tower, the Italianate clock tower built in 1885, is a good spotting landmark. The route is mostly quiet lanes and paths, suitable for a gentle wander or scooters in places, and Cliff Field play area is close by if you want to add a play stop. The village has a pub and a small shop for supplies, and High Tide cafe which sells a brilliant range of sweet treats, breakfast options and light lunch options.

routeDescription: Mincinglake is one of Exeter's quieter green spaces, tucked into a valley with woodland, meadows, a stream and a small play area that feels genuinely separate from the city around it. The stream runs through the bottom of the valley and children who spot it tend to stop and stay for a while. DWT runs free seasonal family activity sessions in summer with bug hunting, birdwatching and nature art, but most days Mincinglake is an unhurried, rustic walk that feels low-key and straightforward if you're in the area.

routeDescription: Dartmeet is where the East and West Dart rivers meet, and for families the appeal is immediate when you arrive: clear, shallow water right next to the car park, giant boulders to climb, stepping stones, grassy riverbanks and the kind of freedom that feels properly Dartmoor. Younger children can spend a happy hour simply paddling, scrambling and throwing stones without going anywhere in particular. The short signed walk north from the car park along the East Dart adds clapper bridges, more climbing, deeper pools and open moorland — and the chance of spotting Dartmoor ponies grazing nearby. The path gets rocky further up so it's not pushchair friendly, but the river stretch near the car park is accessible enough for most families. Toilets and a small café kiosk are at the car park, which makes it easier than many Dartmoor spots to use as a spontaneous stop rather than a planned expedition.

routeDescription: The Castle Feature refers to Woodbury Castle, the Iron Age hillfort that sits at the main car park end of Woodbury Common. It's the most accessible part of the common for families arriving by car — the earthworks are immediately visible from the car park and take only a few minutes to reach on foot. The ramparts and ditches are impressively large up close, and children can scramble along the banks and explore the interior without any formal trail to follow. It works well as a starting point before heading out onto the wider common, or as a standalone short visit if the heathland walk feels like too much.

routeDescription: Denbury Hillfort is a Scheduled Ancient Monument near Newton Abbot, sitting on top of Denbury Down and dating to around 300–100BC. The hillfort is unusually well preserved, with impressive double ramparts and deep ditches on the south and east sides, and two Bronze Age burial mounds inside the fort interior that predate the Iron Age structure itself. Access is via a short ten-minute walk up a lane from the village — narrow and hedged with wildflowers in spring — and the site has interpretation boards explaining what you're looking at. Children can walk the full circumference along the outer ditch path, which takes about twenty minutes and gives a real sense of the scale of the earthworks. In spring the woodland floor inside the fort fills with bluebells. Local legend says a golden crown is buried somewhere on Denbury Down, which is a fun detail mentioning to children before you set off to add an extra spark to the trip.
